abstract: Mitochondrial remodelling is a key feature of neurogenesis in cortical and hippocampal neuronal lineages, yet the temporal control of organellar homeostasis in developing human motor neurons remains poorly understood. Here, we generated a high-resolution temporal resource integrating proteomics, metabolomics, and mitochondrial characterization across human iPSC-to-motor neuron differentiation. This analysis revealed prolonged mitochondrial depletion during early neurogenesis, characterized by reduced mitochondrial content, mitochondrial fragmentation, and lysosome-dependent turnover. This state persisted throughout the neural progenitor stage and was followed by recovery of mitochondrial content during neuronal maturation. During this transition, pyruvate utilization shifted from pyruvate carboxylation towards pyruvate dehydrogenase-dependent oxidation. Pharmacological manipulation of pyruvate partitioning demonstrated that this metabolic switch is required for human neuronal differentiation. Our findings establish a temporal framework for the metabolic control of human motor neuron differentiation and reveal a progenitor-specific state linking mitochondrial depletion to pyruvate metabolism.
